stimulus.source_note: George Washington, Farewell Address, September 17, 1796, public domain. Spelling modernized.
stimulus.text: “The great rule of conduct for us, in regard to foreign nations, is, in extending our commercial relations, to have with them as little political connection as possible. So far as we have already formed engagements, let them be fulfilled with perfect good faith. Here let us stop.” — George Washington, Farewell Address, September 17, 1796

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain excerpt from Washington's Farewell Address (1796)
stem: In the same address, Washington also warned against “the spirit of party.” Which of the following best explains why his warnings about foreign alliances and about parties belong together in one farewell?

options.text: Washington believed the United States should join a permanent alliance with Britain to keep the parties in check at home.
options.misconception: Washington warned against permanent alliances with any nation, including Britain.

options.text: Both warnings are about the same danger: a passionate attachment to a party or a foreign nation overruling the nation's judgment.
Washington was speaking only to the Federalists, who were the only party that favored foreign alliances.
options.misconception: Both parties had foreign attachments — Federalists toward Britain, Democratic-Republicans toward France.

options.text: Washington wanted the president, not Congress, to control both foreign policy and the party system.
options.misconception: The address defends the constitutional system, not presidential control over parties.

rationales.A: Washington warned against permanent alliances with any nation, including Britain.
rationales.B: Washington's address treats party spirit and foreign attachments as two forms of the same disease: a passionate loyalty that makes Americans serve something other than their own country's interest. Background: in the 1790s the Federalists leaned toward Britain and the Democratic-Republicans toward revolutionary France, and each side accused the other of taking foreign orders. Washington's rule is one rule for both dangers — trade with all, ally with none, and let no faction or foreign friend do the nation's thinking for it.
rationales.C: Both parties had foreign attachments — Federalists toward Britain, Democratic-Republicans toward France.
rationales.D: The address defends the constitutional system, not presidential control over parties.
rationales.general:
1. Read the warning again. Trade with everyone, but “as little political connection as possible” — the rule is independence.
2. Ask what party spirit does. It makes a faction's victory matter more than the country's good — the same surrender of judgment Washington fears abroad.
3. Look at the 1790s. Federalists leaned to Britain, Democratic-Republicans to France, and each accused the other of foreign loyalties.
4. Put it together. One farewell, one fear: that Americans would stop thinking for themselves.
Remember: Washington's two warnings are one warning — never let a passion, at home or abroad, choose for you.
